- The method assumes the basis reconstruction function is differentiable; if the underlying basis function has discontinuous derivatives, the resulting gradient will also be discontinuous [S1][S3, unofficial].

The claim states that the method assumes the basis reconstruction function is differentiable and that discontinuous derivatives in the basis function lead to discontinuous gradients. Source [S1] explicitly states that 'Analytic gradients are not continuously differentiable' and that 'Basis reconstruction is continuous, but not continuously differentiable, leading to shading artifacts'. Source [S3] reinforces this by stating, 'If a reconstruction filter with a continuous derivative is not used, the congruent volume gradient will be discontinuous, leading to visible artefacts,' and notes that for linear interpolation (which has a discontinuous derivative), 'the gradient is piece-wise constant... making it discontinuous.' Both sources confirm that the continuity of the gradient depends on the continuity of the derivative of the reconstruction function.

Compute the gradient component $\frac{\partial B(p)}{\partial x}$ using the quotient rule formula [S1].

The claim states that the gradient component ∂B(p)/∂x is computed using the quotient rule formula [S1]. The provided text in Section 5.1.2 explicitly presents Equation (3) for ∂B(p)/∂x. This equation takes the form (u*v' - u*v')/v^2, which is the standard quotient rule for differentiating a ratio (specifically, the derivative of a weighted sum divided by the sum of weights). The text explicitly labels this as the analytic gradient approach derived from the basis reconstruction method. Therefore, the evidence supports the claim that this specific formula (the quotient rule application shown) is used to compute the gradient.

It is distinguished from its parent method, [Gradient Computation via Finite Differences](1077-gradient-computation-via-finite-differences.md), by calculating gradients from existing data values rather than sampling offset positions, and from [Analytic Gradient Computation via Box-Spline Derivatives](3199-analytic-gradient-computation-via-box-spline-derivatives.md) by its general applicability to standard basis reconstruction without relying on specific FCC lattice symmetries [S1].

The claim states that the method is distinguished from [Gradient Computation via Finite Differences] by calculating gradients from existing data values rather than sampling offset positions. This part is supported by Source [S1], which notes that analytic gradients use 'only existing data values' while central differencing (finite differences) 'requires 6 additional basis reconstruction samples at positions offset from the current sample'. However, the claim also states that the method is distinguished from [Analytic Gradient Computation via Box-Spline Derivatives] by its 'general applicability to standard basis reconstruction without relying on specific FCC lattice symmetries'. Source [S1] does not mention 'FCC lattice symmetries' or compare the method to a specific 'Box-Spline Derivatives' method in that context. It only compares analytic gradients to central differences. Therefore, the second part of the claim is not supported by the provided evidence.
